questions.knowledge_point: Converting From Polar Form to Cartesian Form
questions.worked_solution:
To express the number in Cartesian form, we expand the parentheses and substitute the values of the cosine and sine.

Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{6}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{6}=\frac{1}{2}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})) \\  & =2(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\text{i}\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}+\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

To express the number in Cartesian form, we expand the parentheses and substitute the values of the cosine and sine.

First, we find $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the values and expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4})) \\  & =\sqrt{2}(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\text{i}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-1+\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To express the number in Cartesian form, we expand the parentheses and substitute the values of the cosine and sine.

First, we find $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the values and expand the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =16(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})) \\  & =16(\frac{1}{2}-\text{i}\,\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{16}{2}-\text{i}\,\frac{16\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =8-8\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Quotient of Complex Numbers in Polar Form
questions.problem:
Express $z=\frac{6}{1+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give the **exact** values of $r$ and $\theta ,$ in **radians** from $[0,2\pi ).$

$z=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(${{field-2}}$)+i\operatorname{sin}⁡(${{field-3}}$))$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $1-\sqrt{3}\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{6}{1+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{6(1-\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})}{(1+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})(1-\sqrt{3}\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6(1-\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})}{{1}^{2}-(\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6(1-\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})}{1-(-3)} \\  & =\frac{6(1-\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}+\frac{27}{4}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\frac{3}{2}>0$ and $y=-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}<0,$ $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{|y|}{x}) \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}}{\frac{3}{2}}) \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=3(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{3}))
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $4-2\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{3-5\text{i}}{4+2\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{(3-5\text{i})(4-2\text{i})}{(4+2\text{i})(4-2\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{12-6\text{i}-20\text{i}+10{\text{i}}^{2}}{{4}^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{12-26\text{i}-10}{16-(-4)} \\  & =\frac{2-26\text{i}}{20} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}-\frac{13}{10}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{1}{10}-\frac{13}{10}\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{10})}^{2}+{(-\frac{13}{10})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1+169}{100}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{170}{100}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{170}}{10} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{170}}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\frac{1}{10}$ and $y=-\frac{13}{10},$ $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{|y|}{x}) \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\frac{13}{10}}{\frac{1}{10}}) \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡(13) \\  & ≈2\pi -1.49 \\  & ≈4.79,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places. 

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=\frac{\sqrt{170}}{10}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4.79)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4.79))
$$
